doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Concord, one-take recording, and Dick Gibson's jazz party
summary: They record with Concord, with no rehearsal and one take, and Dick Gibson was surprised Jeannie played piano and sang.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: And you’ve been with a couple of different record labels.
Not really. Concord is our main one.
In terms of our own individual, Concord was the initiator.
When you record, this is almost a silly question in some cases, but do you all play at the same time?

Well the main thing, they never see the arrangements until they get to the studio. We never rehearse. And most of the stuff we did was one take. Very seldom we had to do two takes, which kept the stuff edgy and fresh.
But I mean you don’t record the rhythm section and then do the vocals?
Oh, no.
I mean, I knew the answer to that because I could tell. © Fillius Jazz Archive -31-
Well a lot of people didn’t. Because Dick, up in Denver that used to do the jazz parties?
Dick Gibson.

Dick Gibson, when we came up there to do his jazz party, he insisted, on, “I have a good piano player for you.” I said, “I’m the piano player.” He said, “You didn’t do it on your records.” He had been playing our records for about four years on his radio show.
Yeah, you’re right.
And I said, “I’ve always played my—” He said, “You never did that.” I said, “Look at the record.” I always play my own music and I never do it and then sing, I always do it at the same time.
Simultaneously.
And so he said, “I’ve got a wonderful piano player for you.” I said, “Well I’m going to be it. I’m it.”
It shook him up.
He didn’t want me to play.
Because he had his own —
He had his own idea about who.
It was his plantation.
Well it was. Shifting everybody around, you play this—
He has control, because you play over here and put this one—
And this one with that one and that one, whether they fit or not.
Yeah, that can be a dicey way to play.
Well, it’s a challenge. Those guys came through like champs, because they’re all good you know, and they knew it was just a gig.

But at the same time, the most beautiful thing about it, the caliber of jazz musicians involved you see, they know, they’d met grace, and they know grace. They’ve been all over the world and they played kings and queens and etcetera. Shahs, and just name it. So there’s no way in the world he could shake them up. No way. They’d just give him that grace period.

I’ve enjoyed hearing from people like Clark Terry and basically what you’re saying, that a lot of the musicians I’ve spoken to along the way have met with either racial or other obstacles along the way, and that they’ve said to themselves, no way is this going to change me. It’s your problem, and I’m comfortable with myself.
